name: Hypothesis Deep

stars.name: The Metronome
stars.notes: A millisecond pulsar spinning 173 times per second, the most precise natural clock in charted space; its beam sweeps the system like a lighthouse with an agenda, and every experiment here is ultimately synchronized to it.

planets.name: Anvil
planets.notes: A dead iron world stripped bare by the supernova that birthed the pulsar; its surface is fused glass to a depth of ten meters, and probes sent there stop transmitting within hours.

planets.name: Crucible Minor
planets.notes: A dense fragment of the original star's companion, half-vaporized and re-frozen; its composition should not exist, which is exactly why three laboratories compete to sample it.

anomalies.name: The Stutter
anomalies.location: near star, along the radiation axis
anomalies.notes: A narrow zone where clock drift exceeds relativistic predictions by a fixed, reproducible factor. Instruments run fast inside it. So, according to two verified logs, do people.

anomalies.name: Deep Masque
anomalies.notes: A gravitational mass with no visible source, roughly lunar in effect; it orbits nothing, drifts a few meters a year, and has been weighed more accurately than most planets.

stations.name: Second Hand Station
stations.notes: The system's only habitation: a shielded physics platform where consortium teams run timing experiments in shifts. Its corridors are windowless by design, and its clocks are checked against each other hourly.

stations.name: Array Null
stations.notes: An automated gravimetric array watching the invisible mass; a skeleton crew of four rotates through every six months and reports, without exception, that they dislike it there.

faction_control.notes: No flag flies here. Three research consortia share the chartered volume under the Interstitial Accords, and the standing joke is that the pulsar outranks them all: its schedule is the only law everyone obeys.

history: The pulsar was charted during the first timing surveys and immediately declared a shared scientific reserve after two navies nearly came to blows over who would control its signal.
The Stutter was confirmed fourteen years ago when a probe returned from the radiation axis with data that matched no relativity model but matched itself perfectly on every repeat run.
Last year Array Null recorded the Deep Masque changing course by a fraction of a degree, the first movement in its observed history, toward the inner system.
description: One star, or what is left of one: a white point spinning faster than machinery, sweeping its beam across two scorched remnants of worlds. The system is small, hard, and quiet in the way of places that have already had their catastrophe. Everything that could burn here did, long ago.

What remains is precision. Three hundred researchers rotate through Second Hand Station, running experiments that depend on the Metronome's beat being exactly what it has always been, and forty more tend the array that watches an invisible mass hang in the outer dark. Traffic is a supply run every few weeks; the consortium charter forbids anything louder than science.

But the precision is starting to crack at the edges. The Stutter's clock drift is fixed, reproducible, and wrong. The Masque, motionless for all recorded history, has begun to move. And the station's oldest in-joke, that you can set your watch by the pulsar, has gone quiet among the senior staff, because lately some of their watches disagree about how long a shift has been.
